title: Before You Grow, Define What the Business Should Give You
description: Growth is a route, not a personal objective. Define what your business should make possible before committing to its next stage.

sections.heading: Start with the outcome
paragraphs: “I want to grow the business” sounds like a clear objective. It still leaves the most important question unanswered: what do you expect that growth to change for you?

More personal income? A business that can operate without your daily involvement? Greater control? The ability to build something larger? These are different outcomes. A route that serves one can work against another.

In ENDGAME, the proposed starting point is the owner's personal objective. The business strategy follows from that objective, alongside the company's obligations and the rights and interests of its other owners. That is not a licence to put one person's wishes above everyone else. It is a way to make the starting point explicit before the decisions become expensive to reverse.

sections.heading: Replace the ambition with a destination
paragraphs: Start with a sentence you could assess later:
“By this date, I want this personal outcome, measured in this way.”

Now add two lines: what you are prepared to contribute or give up, and what you are not prepared to accept. You do not need a perfect forecast. You need a useful distinction between the result you want and a route you currently find attractive.

For example, “work no more than two operational days a week within eighteen months” is different from “hire a managing director.” The first describes an intended personal outcome. The second proposes a means of getting there. Hiring someone does not, by itself, establish that the owner has become less involved.

sections.heading: Check the price of success
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical founder whose goal is greater operational independence. An investor offers expansion capital on the condition that the founder remains in a full-time executive role for several more years.

The offer may be commercially attractive. It may also conflict with the founder's stated objective. A sound decision would compare the actual obligations with that objective, rather than treat obtaining the investment as a victory in itself.
The useful question is not only “What happens if this fails?” It is also “What will this require from me if it succeeds?”

A new commitment might be acceptable. The founder may decide that building a larger company now is more important than stepping back soon. That can be a coherent choice. The point is to acknowledge the trade-off, update the objective and avoid pretending that both priorities were fulfilled without compromise.

sections.heading: Put the other owners into the picture
paragraphs: Your personal objective is a starting point, not a decision-making right. Other shareholders may want different things, and the business has commitments of its own.

Write down what you know about those positions. Keep confirmed interests separate from assumptions. Identify the decisions you can make, the agreements you need and the questions that require professional advice.

This may reveal that your objective is compatible with the existing arrangement. It may reveal a negotiable difference. It may also show that a particular route depends on an agreement you do not yet have. Each finding changes the next move.

sections.heading: Choose a move you can test
paragraphs: Before approving a major change, ask what evidence would show that the route is working.

For the hypothetical founder seeking independence, a useful first move might be a clearly bounded delegation trial. Record operational time, the decisions that still return to the founder and the quality of the work. Agree beforehand which decisions the team can make and what must be escalated.

The trial is not a promise that delegation will work. It is a way to examine the conditions under which it could work. If the same decisions keep coming back, investigate why rather than declaring success because a new job title exists.

sections.heading: Four questions before the next commitment
paragraphs: What do I personally want the business to make possible?
Which interests, rights and constraints shape the available routes?
What does the next move require from me if it works—and what remains if it does not?
What evidence will tell us that I am closer to the intended outcome?

That is the logic of GOAL, POSITION, MOVE and OUTCOME. ENDGAME is a developing personal strategy model, not a guarantee of success or a substitute for specialist advice. Its practical purpose is to keep the desired outcome visible while the strategy is being built.
A bigger business can be the right ambition. Make sure it is connected to the outcome you actually choose.
